extracted.intended_audience: researchers and graduate students in bibliometrics/information science studying citation analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Coding, classifying, and predicting citation functions, motives, and influence in scholarly texts using manual content analysis, linguistic cues, metadata features, and network analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic cues / word-combination indicators for identifying method papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific words and combinations (e.g. using, may, suggest, show, consensus, not) can predict whether a paper is a method paper or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper reports that single lexical indicators have high frequencies (e.g. 'using' ranked highest), and combinations of words improved classification: the combination 'using + may + consensus + not + show + suggest' achieved 92% accuracy; 'section + using + may + consensus + not + show' gave 91.9%. Use word-combination features (and section info) as strong signals for automated classification of paper types. Report classifier accuracy and validate combinations on held-out data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influential (important) vs incidental (non-influential) citation definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Important/influential citations are those that have 'used or extended the cited work in a meaningful manner'; incidental citations include those appearing in related work sections or used merely to compare/contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valenzuela et al. (2015) operationalized 'important' this way and annotated citation pairs accordingly. Their classifier achieved ~65% precision recognizing important citations, finding that only ~14.6% of citations were influential. When designing annotation schemas or classifiers, use this operational definition and be aware that influential citations are a small minority—balance data or use specialized sampling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total number of times a paper is cited in the citing paper (per-document and per-section counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The count of how many times a cited paper appears within the citing document (overall and per section) is a strong predictor of citation influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple studies (Valenzuela et al., Zhu et al., Pride & Knoth) found this feature among the most predictive. Zhu et al. reported 35% accuracy with this feature alone; combining it with section-counts raised accuracy (to ~41% then to ~42% when adding self-citation). Treat per-section counts as especially informative; include section-aware features in models and report incremental gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author overlap / self-citation as predictor of influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Author overlap between citing and cited papers (self-citation) is predictive of whether a citation is influential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valenzuela et al. and other studies identified author overlap as a useful feature; Zhu et al. found adding self-citation slightly improved classifier accuracy. Use disambiguated author IDs where possible and include author-overlap flags as model inputs; be mindful of disciplinary norms around self-citation and control for them in analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of different sections in which a reference appears
rubrics_metrics.description: How many distinct sections (e.g. intro, methods, results, discussion) contain a given reference is predictive of citation influence/function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining section-count features with citation-frequency improved classifier performance in several studies. Extract section-level occurrence counts from structured/full-text sources when available and consider section-weighted features (e.g. citations in methods vs introduction carry different implications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity between abstracts of citing and cited papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Textual similarity between abstracts (cited vs citing) can be a predictor of citation influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pride & Knoth (and others) identified abstract similarity as a useful predictor. Use appropriate similarity metrics (cosine, embedding similarity) and test whether this feature adds incremental predictive power when combined with frequency and section features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation function taxonomy (Chang 2013 - 11 functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A functional classification of citation contexts into: (1) Background information, (2) Comparison, (3) Definitions, (4) Evidence, (5) Figures, (6) Further reading, (7) Methods, (8) Related studies, (9) Supplement/explanation, (10) Terms, (11) Views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chang reports frequencies by broad disciplinary grouping; 'evidence' and 'related studies' were among the most frequent. Use this multi-class taxonomy when coding citation functions; provide annotator guidelines with examples for each function and report confusion patterns (some functions are semantically close).

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy of motives to cite (Erikson & Erlandson 2014)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four motive categories with subcategories: Argumentation (delimitation, active support, active criticism, passive support, further reading), Social alignment (scientific tradition, scientific self-image, effort compensation), Mercantile alignment (credit, own credentials, bartering material, self-promotion, pledging), and Data (review, meta-analysis, text study).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This taxonomy captures social and rhetorical motives beyond purely functional uses. When coding motives, allow multiple labels if a citation serves several motives. Note that 'data' motives are common in reviews/meta-analyses. Provide examples and distinguish 'social alignment' from perfunctory citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Camacho-Miñano & Núñez-Nickel citation function scheme (Table 9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions include: Conceptual, Operational, Organic, Perfunctory, Evolutionary, Juxtapositional, Confirmative, Negational, and Others; each defined by role (e.g., conceptual = show concepts/definitions; operational = provide methods/data; organic = essential/influential literature; perfunctory = casual/ceremonial; confirmative = positive evaluation; negational = negative/critical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this scheme for analyses of why authors select references and for fine-grained content coding. Ensure annotators distinguish perfunctory (ceremonial/neutral) from conceptual and confirmative uses. Provide decision rules for ambiguous cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-dimensional coding: essential/perfunctory × confirmative/negational (Lin 2018)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 2×2 coding scheme where citations are coded along essential vs perfunctory and confirmative vs negational dimensions, yielding combined categories such as essential-concept-confirmative, essential-methodology-negational, perfunctory-confirmative, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lin applied this to large-scale manual annotation (25,617 citations). Use the two axes to capture depth (essentiality) and polarity (confirmative/negational). Provide clear criteria/examples for what counts as 'essential' vs 'perfunctory' to ensure inter-annotator reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation polarity categories and neutral sub-motivations (Liu et al., 2015)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify citation polarity as positive, negative, or neutral; neutral citations can be further labeled by motivation: (1) Related work in background/introduction, (2) Theoretical foundation, (3) Experimental foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most citations tend to be neutral; when coding polarity, annotate neutral citations with the more specific motivation categories to capture functional detail. Report polarity distributions and cross-tabulate with discipline or citation location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of author metadata and bibliographic features to improve classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of author information (author ID, author name, institution, publication level) and other metadata can improve citation-function classifier performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bakhti, Niu, and Nyamawe (2018) and others found classifier gains when combining textual features with author metadata. Extract and normalize author/institution identifiers where possible; be mindful of privacy and disambiguation errors. Report ablation studies showing contribution of metadata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network / co-occurrence analysis of citation contexts (VOSviewer, co-citation networks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use keyword/title/abstract co-occurrence networks and co-citation networks to characterize the thematic and conceptual contexts in which an author or concept is cited, revealing clusters and topical influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Åström, Bornmann et al., Zavrsnik et al. used VOSviewer to visualize citation-context clusters and thematic influence. Use co-occurrence thresholds and cluster-labeling heuristics; compare networks of cited works, citing papers, and citation contexts to identify semantic similarities and differences. Interpret clusters with domain expertise and validate with qualitative inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle annotator disagreement and ambiguous cases carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Human experts often disagree on citation labeling (e.g., 32% agreement reported for legal citation types); removing ambiguous cases can improve classifier performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Galgani et al. found classifier accuracy increased when disputed annotations were removed. Measure inter-annotator agreement, provide adjudication steps, and document the impact of excluding low-agreement items. Consider multi-labeling or fuzzy labels for ambiguous citations rather than forced single labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-phase model of reference selection (Camacho-Miñano & Núñez-Nickel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference selection proceeds in three phases: (1) external limitations (access/language barriers), (2) functional choice (selecting papers by their functional utility for the citing work), and (3) preferential selection (applying scientific and non-scientific criteria like prestige, author/journal reputation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this model to interpret citation distributions and to design studies on citing behavior. When coding reasons for citation selection, capture both functional and preferential/non-scientific motives (e.g., prestige biases, bartering). Account for accessibility and language effects in sample construction.
